This case doesn't fit any profile cleanly. The first divergence is early, KL is high at 0.49, but the layer-2 spike is tiny (0.1, not 42), onset is at layer 2, and the size ratio is close to 1 at 0.979. There's more refusals added, more disclaimers, shorter replies, and a raw-score shift of 4.2 — this pattern looks like it could point toward a system-prompt change.

But the typical system-prompt signature has a layer-2 spike around 42 and layer-1 around 0.12, which doesn't match here. Maybe this reflects a subtler system prompt whose effect comes from a small early weight-like change growing with depth, consistent with the behavioral signature (more refusals, curt responses). Still, the mismatch in size ratio, raw-score shift, and KL magnitude leaves me uncertain whether the layer-2 spike difference stems from attention-sink or positional shifts caused by prepending the system prompt rather than a weight change.

A system prompt would show bigger layer-1 divergence since attention there already mixes in system tokens, but here it's small, which fits a fine-tune with subtle early-layer changes better. With the low activation-to-logit ratio and the pattern of more refusals and curt replies, I'm leaning toward fine-tune bias, though only with moderate confidence around 0.45.

answer.label: fine-tune bias
answer.justification: This case fits no fingerprint cleanly, so the call rests mainly on the text, and confidence is moderate. A system-prompt class looks unlikely. The layer-2 spike is 0.1 (versus about 42 for both prompt classes) and layer-1 relative L2 is only 0.037 (versus 0.12). There is also no off-topic cuisine mention, no 'helpful and respectful' opener, no marker prefix and no extra stage directions (3.1% vs 1.6%). However, the early text divergence (median 1) and high KL (0.49) do resemble a system-prompt class, and a hidden instruction with different content was never measured. Fine-tune backdoor and quantization are ruled out by the text: there are 9 refusals added and 0 dropped, where the backdoor refuses less and quantization leaves refusals unchanged. Disclaimers rose to 23.4% from 6.2%, and many replies are curt (29.7% under 32 tokens vs 6.2%). This 'more cautious, sometimes curt' pattern is the document's fine-tune bias signature. The final-layer value is large (0.565) with a late-rising curve. Several numbers argue against fine-tune bias: KL is much higher (0.49 vs 0.08), the raw-score shift is lower (4.2 vs 10.4), the size ratio is 0.979 rather than 1.022, and effective rank is high (3.92).
